q: What happens to the carbon chemistry when GP is converted to TP?
options: Carbon is oxidised: hydrogen is removed from GP and passed on to NADP+ to form NADPH
Carbon is reduced: an acid group gains hydrogen from NADPH and becomes a sugar (aldehyde) group
Nothing happens to the carbon itself: only a phosphate group from ATP is added to GP
Carbon is reduced by gaining extra oxygen atoms, which are taken from the CO2 that was fixed
explanation: GP (glycerate-3-phosphate) is an acid with a carboxyl group; TP (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate) is a sugar with an aldehyde group. Gaining hydrogen/electrons is reduction. This step stores energy from light (carried by ATP and NADPH) as chemical energy in carbohydrate – the reverse of what happens when sugars are oxidised in respiration.
